questions.q: What does an Always On Availability Group (AG) actually fail over as a unit?
options: A single table within a database
Only the transaction log, without the data files
A named group of user databases, which fail over together to a secondary replica
The entire SQL Server instance, including system databases
questions.explain: An AG is defined as a group of databases that fail over together — not the whole instance and not an individual table.

questions.q: What is the real trade-off of synchronous commit versus asynchronous commit in an AG?
options: Synchronous commit is always slower and less reliable than asynchronous commit
Asynchronous commit guarantees zero data loss with no latency cost
Synchronous commit gives zero data loss but adds write latency; asynchronous commit has no latency penalty but risks some data loss if the primary fails first
There is no difference — both modes behave identically
questions.explain: Synchronous commit waits for secondary confirmation before committing (safe but slower); asynchronous commits immediately (fast but risks loss).

questions.q: Why is synchronous commit required for automatic failover to be safe?
options: Because asynchronous replicas cannot be promoted under any circumstances
Because it guarantees the secondary already has every committed transaction, so failing over automatically loses nothing
Because automatic failover has nothing to do with commit mode
Because synchronous commit is only available on Azure SQL Database
questions.explain: Automatic failover can only be trusted when the secondary is guaranteed current, which is exactly what synchronous commit ensures.

questions.q: In the lesson's example CREATE AVAILABILITY GROUP statement, why is SQLNODE3-DR configured with ASYNCHRONOUS_COMMIT instead of synchronous?
options: There's no reason — it was chosen arbitrarily
Because asynchronous commit is required for any node named with a "-DR" suffix
Because Azure SQL Managed Instance does not support synchronous commit
Because it's in a different region, and synchronous commit's network round-trip over that distance would make every write unacceptably slow
questions.explain: Asynchronous commit is what you use for a distant replica, where waiting for confirmation over that latency would be unacceptable for every write.

questions.q: Why does ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP ... FAILOVER (without FORCE) only work cleanly against a synchronous replica?
options: Because synchronous replicas cannot actually become the primary
Because FAILOVER without FORCE only works on Azure SQL Database, never on-prem
There's no real distinction between FAILOVER and FORCE_FAILOVER_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS
Because synchronous commit already guarantees the secondary has zero data loss, so a clean failover is safe; forcing failover on an asynchronous replica risks losing committed transactions
questions.explain: FORCE_FAILOVER_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS exists specifically for the disaster case on an asynchronous replica where the primary is unreachable and some loss is accepted.
